summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force since 2 January 2026, penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; prosecution is reported as selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. In Aceh, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is documented and escalating. Reporting on 14 and 15 August 2026 describes vigilante mobs attacking transgender women, with commentators tying the surge to officials' rhetoric and to an October 2025 presidential decree by President Prabowo Subianto listing LGBTQ+ people among nonmilitary national-defense threats alongside separatism and terrorism. An academic commentator stated the regulation shifts rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, framing LGBTQ+ people as risks to be monitored and controlled.

A documented death-in-custody case involved a trans traveller: Harvard student Rodrigo Ventocilla, on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges in August 2022; his mother was told on a WhatsApp call that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, and he died in custody. His mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Venue-based police raids target LGBT gatherings. On 22 June 2025, police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor and arrested 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'; Amnesty International's Wirya Adiwena called the raid a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and said the gathering violated no law.

Expression is censored. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalises any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations, with up to 7 years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal. The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr, and shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni. In 2025 a new bill was under discussion to explicitly prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour.

Discriminatory regulation and arrests have been documented since 2016. HRW reported on 7 July 2026 a surge in abuse against LGBT students following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organisation, documented 94 cases, and in early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'. In August 2016 the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities mental illnesses and recommended psychological rehabilitation, while the government remained mostly silent.

No specific law protects Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2019, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999). The Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting on the August 2026 attacks ties them to the October 2025 presidential decree and to officials' verbal attacks, presenting violence and official framing as one escalation rather than separate phenomena.

HRW has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, indicating a sustained pattern rather than isolated incidents.

The 2016 HRW report identified the government's silence following the psychiatric association's pathologisation as an origin point of an institutionalised anti-LGBT posture, which later reporting in 2025 and 2026 treats as having hardened into codified policy.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender.

Since June 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services.

Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third gender or X option, and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since 2018, the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional,' regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'; officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender.

Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans, and the Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organisation provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic; Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 penal code's extra-marital sex provision has been applied to a trans visitor specifically is unresolved in this record; prosecution is reported as selective, and no trans-specific case under the new code is documented here.

The current enforcement posture of the 2015 police circular on hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009, is not sourced beyond their issuance; no data on outcomes is available.

The 2025 bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour is described as under discussion; its enactment status is unresolved in this record.

The Harvard Crimson's account of a US$100,000 demand and of police beating Ventocilla rests on his mother's allegations, which Indonesian police deny; the discrepancy is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator and period is available in this inventory, so no comparative rate against Indonesia's general homicide rate can be stated.
